transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, it's nice to meet you too. Um, so, I guess what finally made me actually make this appointment and come in today is... well, I'm 22, I finished my degree, and I'm supposed to be, you know, transitioning into the real world and being independent, but I am just completely failing at it. I keep forgetting basic adult things, and it's getting really, really out of hand. 

Like, paying bills, for example. I'll have the money sitting right there in my checking account, but I just completely forget to actually log in and hit the pay button until I get slapped with a late fee. And it's not just the little things, it's important stuff too, like returning interview emails. I'll see an email from a job I applied to, and I'll think, "Okay, I need to sit down and write a really professional response to this," and then... I don't know, I put my phone down to do something else, and I completely forget the email even exists for like a week. By the time I remember, the position is already filled. It has started costing me real opportunities, and it's just so incredibly frustrating. 

It's the same thing with showing up for appointments—I completely blank on them, or I swear they were scheduled for a different day, and I leave people hanging. And errands! I'll leave the house specifically to do one thing, like drop off a package, and I'll end up driving around doing three other random things and never actually follow through on the one errand I left the house for. It's just... it's ruining my life right now, honestly, because I can't seem to just function and remember to do the things I desperately need to do.
Did you have these same kinds of attention and forgetfulness problems when you were a child?

Oh, wow, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It's funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this the other day, and she actually pulled out this old box of my report cards from elementary school. And honestly, reading through them, it was like looking at the exact same person I am right now, just smaller. 

Like, my second-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins—I still remember her, she was so sweet but I drove her crazy—she wrote this whole paragraph about how I was, you know, a "bright" student, which they always say, but then she went on and on about how I was constantly losing my worksheets. Like, literally every single day. She'd hand it out, and five minutes later, I'd have no idea where it went. And it wasn't just losing things; it was the way I did everything. She noted that I always rushed through directions. I would just glance at the top of the page, assume I knew exactly what to do, and then do the whole assignment completely wrong because I didn't actually read the instructions. 

And the talking! Oh my gosh, every single report card said something about me talking out of turn. I just couldn't hold it in. If I had a thought, it had to come out of my mouth right that second, even if the teacher was right in the middle of a sentence. I just... I didn't even realize I was doing it half the time until they called my name. 

And my desk... oh, my desk was a disaster zone. It was famous in the class. It was just this black hole of crumpled papers, broken crayons, half-eaten snacks, and lost homework. Mrs. Higgins actually wrote that my desk was so messy I could never find my assignments when it was time to turn them in. We'd have "desk clean-out day" on Fridays, and it would take me the entire period just to sort through the chaos, and by Monday, it was completely destroyed again. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing. It's just... back then, the consequences were a bad grade or missing recess, and now the consequences are, you know, my actual life falling apart. But the core stuff? The losing things, the rushing, the talking, the mess? That's been me literally since I can remember.
As a child, were you often unable to stay seated when you were expected to?

Um, staying seated? Actually, no, I don't think that was really my thing. Like, I don't remember ever getting in trouble for getting up and wandering around or anything like that. 

It's kind of weird, right, because you'd think with all the talking and the massive mess I just told you about, I'd be all over the place, but I actually usually stayed right in my chair. I remember my third-grade classroom had this really strict seating chart—we were in these little pods of four desks pushed together, you know how they do?—and I would just sit there. I mean, I wasn't doing my work, obviously. I was probably staring out the window or whispering to the girl across from me, but I wasn't physically leaving my seat. 

There was this one kid in my class, I think his name was Tyler, and he was always getting up to go to the pencil sharpener or the trash can, like literally every five minutes. I remember just watching him and getting completely sidetracked by his whole routine, just tracking him across the room instead of doing my math, but I never really did that myself. I think I was just too caught up in whatever chaotic thing was happening right in front of me at my own desk to bother getting up. 

So, yeah, as far as actually getting up when I wasn't supposed to, I don't think I did that. Or at least, my mom didn't mention it, and it definitely wasn't in those report cards she showed me. It was mostly just the talking out of turn and the disorganized disaster of my desk, but I was pretty anchored to the chair while all that was happening.
As a child, did you often run around or climb on things when it wasn’t appropriate?

Climbing on things? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, my mom was pretty strict about how we behaved indoors, so if I ever tried to scale the bookshelves or run laps around a restaurant, she would have completely shut that down immediately. So I wasn't really a climber, and like I said, I stayed in my chair at school. 

But it's actually really interesting you bring up that kind of physical energy, because... well, even if I'm not literally running around, I have this... this feeling, and it's honestly one of the most exhausting things I deal with, especially right now with trying to find a job. 

It's less about running and more about this intense, trapped feeling. When I have to sit through an interview, or a meeting, or honestly, even just a movie... I feel this pressure inside my body. It's like my blood is carbonated or something, I don't even know how to explain it properly. I just feel this absolute, desperate need to get up, or shift around, or do something with my hands, or I will literally crawl out of my skin. 

Like, my friends and I went to see a movie a couple weeks ago, one of those really long three-hour ones, and everyone else was just completely engrossed, eating their popcorn, perfectly still. And I was just sitting there in the dark, constantly crossing and uncrossing my legs, messing with my cuticles, shifting my weight, just praying for it to end because the physical requirement of just staying in that one plush seat was taking every single ounce of willpower I had. It's like the longer I have to stay put and be "professional" or "quiet," the more this pressure just builds and builds in my chest and my arms. It takes so much mental energy just to stop myself from standing up and pacing around the room. So, no, I wasn't swinging from the chandeliers as a kid or anything, but that physical restlessness is definitely there. It's just... it's all trapped inside me, I guess, and it makes doing normal adult things feel physically painful.
As a child, did adults often describe you as always being "on the go" or like you were driven by a motor?

Driven by a motor... oh my gosh, yes. My mom used to say I was like a wind-up toy that someone overwound and just let loose in the house. She was always telling me to just pause for one second, but I couldn't. 

And honestly, it hasn't stopped at all. It's actually kind of ridiculous because, like I mentioned, I just graduated and I don't even have a job right now, so you'd think my days would be pretty chill, right? Like I'd just be relaxing or watching TV or something. But no. Even without a job right now, I move from one thing to the next all day long. It is just constant. 

Like, a typical day for me... I'll start the morning thinking, okay, I need to do laundry. So I grab the basket, but on the way down the hall, I realize I need to check my emails to see if any of those jobs got back to me. So I drop the laundry basket—literally just abandon it right in the middle of the floor—and open my laptop. But then I see my browser is a complete disaster, so I spend, I don't know, an hour just reorganizing my tabs, trying to sort them into different windows. And then I get this overwhelming urge to just... move. So I get up and start pacing. I'll just pace around my apartment, back and forth, thinking about all the other things I should be doing instead of the tabs. And then suddenly it's late afternoon and I think, oh shoot, I need to eat, so I run to the kitchen to start dinner and start pulling out pots and pans and ingredients. 

It's like... I cannot let myself stop. My body just won't allow me to sit and just be. I have to be doing something, moving, shifting to the next task, going, going, going. It feels exactly like a motor that's just idling too high. And the absolute most frustrating part of the whole thing is that I do all of this, I am going at a hundred miles an hour from the second I wake up, but none of it actually gets finished! Like, at the end of the day, the laundry is still sitting in the hallway, the important emails aren't sent, and dinner is just half-chopped vegetables sitting on the counter. But I've been completely exhausted by being on the go the entire time. So yeah, that motor thing
